::: {.callout-important}
## Document authority

This is the canonical description of the logical system. It governs system
behavior, trust boundaries, human approval, lifecycle transitions, and the
minimum contracts between components. The canonical GMD schema remains the
authority for statistical definitions. Infrastructure products are governed
by `infrastructure-requirements.qmd` and are not fixed by this document.
:::

# Purpose and status

The GMD AI-assisted harmonization system is intended to reduce the repetitive
work required to interpret and standardize household survey microdata while
preserving methodological authority, reproducibility, and auditability.

The system separates three responsibilities:

1. AI-assisted interpretation produces structured proposals and diagnostics.
2. Human experts make and approve methodological decisions.
3. Fixed, versioned code executes approved decisions deterministically.

This document consolidates the stable logic found across the project's concept
notes, process narratives, infrastructure requests, and presentations. Where
those drafts conflicted, this document adopts the stricter governance rule and
records unresolved matters explicitly.

::: {.callout-note}
## Terminology

This repository uses **Global Micro Database (GMD)**, matching the project
charter. Archived drafts also use "Global Monitoring Database."

# Scope

## Objectives

The system is designed to:

- shorten the time between survey intake and a reviewable harmonization draft;
- improve consistency across surveys and waves;
- make mappings, transformations, overrides, and reasons explicit;
- execute accepted logic reproducibly;
- preserve quality-assured decisions as searchable institutional knowledge;
  and
- support a controlled transition away from opaque survey-specific scripts.

These are intended outcomes, not measured benefits. Efficiency or quality
claims require a defined evaluation and evidence from the proof of concept.

## Non-goals

The system is not intended to:

- delegate final methodological authority to an AI model;
- execute unapproved logic in production;
- infer a new GMD methodology from historical frequency;
- treat a past decision as binding when it conflicts with the current schema;
- put methodology exclusively in model weights or prompts;
- store raw microdata in this architecture repository; or
- select cloud products before institutional, security, and operational review.

# Architecture invariants

The following properties are mandatory unless the accountable governance body
formally changes this architecture:

1. **Schema authority.** The approved GMD schema and methodology override
   historical precedents, model suggestions, and implementation convenience.
2. **Human authority.** An accountable human expert approves every
   methodological specification before production execution.
3. **Separation of decision and execution.** AI may propose and diagnose;
   deterministic code applies the exact approved specification.
4. **Immutable approval.** Approval applies to one content-addressed version.
   Any change to mappings, transformations, rules, or executable logic creates
   a new version and requires approval again.
5. **Reproducible lineage.** A production result identifies immutable input
   versions, specification version and hash, schema version, engine version,
   configuration, dependency environment, and QA policy version.
6. **Explicit failure.** Missing required inputs, invalid contracts, failed
   checks, and unresolved ambiguities stop or route the workflow visibly. They
   do not trigger silent defaults.
7. **Controlled model boundary.** Raw respondent-level microdata is not sent to
   a language model by default. Any exception requires documented data-owner,
   security, and infrastructure approval.
8. **Governed learning.** Only human-approved decisions that pass the required
   QA and precedent-admission checks can enter the reusable precedent base.
9. **Auditability.** Material inputs, model outputs, review actions, execution
   events, QA results, and publication decisions have attributable records.
10. **Repository separation.** This hub documents the system but does not store
    operational code, secrets, or survey data.

# System context and ownership

The system consists of capabilities, not necessarily one application or one
repository. Product and repository boundaries may change without changing the
logical architecture.

| Capability | Owns | Must not own |
|---|---|---|
| Canonical GMD schema | Variable definitions, derivation rules, constraints, schema versions | Survey-specific proposals or historical exceptions |
| Intake and profiling | Source registration, immutable file identity, deterministic data profiles | Methodological approval |
| Documentation extraction | Structured metadata with provenance and extraction confidence | Unreviewed claims that extracted metadata is official DDI |
| Historical precedents | Searchable approved decisions and their lineage | Canonical methodology |
| Drafting and diagnosis | Candidate mappings, evidence, uncertainty, bounded diagnostics | Approval or production authorization |
| Human review | Acceptance, rejection, correction, justification, sign-off | Silent mutation of already approved versions |
| Harmonization engine | Deterministic application of an authorized specification | Interpretation or discretionary fallback |
| QA and publication | Versioned checks, explicit disposition, release record | Automatic acceptance of failed output |
| Harmonization Hub | Cross-system architecture, contracts, decisions, rationale | Pipeline code or microdata |

# Information sources and authority

The drafting process draws on four source classes:

| Source | Role | Authority |
|---|---|---|
| Raw survey microdata | Factual record of observed values and structure | Authoritative for what the delivered file contains, subject to provenance checks |
| Survey documentation | Meaning, questionnaire design, codes, universe, and methodology | Source-dependent; preserve provenance and uncertainty |
| Canonical GMD schema and guidelines | Target definitions, constraints, and derivations | Binding |
| Approved historical decisions | Relevant examples and expert reasoning from prior cases | Advisory |

Retrieved precedents must carry citations to their originating approval and QA
records. A precedent that conflicts with the current schema is flagged; it is
never used to override the schema.

# Trust boundaries and data flow

Different components need different views of survey information. Access must be
least-privilege and based on classification rather than convenience.

| Information | Controlled storage | Profiler or executor | Model service | Human reviewer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Raw respondent-level microdata | Required | Allowed in approved environment | Prohibited by default | Only through approved analytical access |
| Survey documents and DDI | Required | Allowed | Open pending classification and model-service approval | Allowed according to source controls |
| Aggregated data profile | Required | Produced | Open pending field-level disclosure policy | Allowed according to classification |
| Canonical schema | Required | Allowed | Allowed | Allowed |
| Approved precedents | Required | Allowed as needed | Allowed subject to classification | Allowed |
| Draft and approved specifications | Required | Draft only in sandbox; approved in production | Draft access only | Allowed |
| Diagnostics and logs | Required with retention controls | Produced | Only an approved, minimized diagnostic subset | Allowed by role |

An AI-controlled process may request sandbox execution, but the sandbox executor
is the component that reads microdata. Only diagnostics allowed by the data-flow
policy may return to the model. The exact aggregation, suppression, logging, and
retention rules are open infrastructure and data-governance decisions.

# Canonical lifecycle

The lifecycle is a state machine. Inputs are sources, not stages, and feedback
loops are transitions rather than additional stage numbers.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    I[Intake and register sources] --> P[Profile data and structure documentation]
    P --> D[Draft specification]
    D --> T[Bounded pre-approval validation or sandbox testing]
    T -->|criteria met or stop condition| R[Human review]
    T -->|repair permitted| D
    R -->|reject with reason| D
    R -->|approve exact version| E[Deterministic production execution]
    E --> Q[Quality assurance]
    Q -->|pass| U[Publish output and audit record]
    Q -->|fail| X[Human disposition]
    X -->|unchanged technical retry| E
    X -->|logic change required| D
    U --> A[Precedent admission review]
    A -->|admit| H[Approved precedent base]
    A -->|do not admit| Z[Retain run lineage only]
```

## Intake and structuring

The system registers source files with stable identifiers, hashes, provenance,
classification, and access policy. Deterministic profiling summarizes the raw
data. Documentation extraction produces structured metadata while retaining a
link to the original source and extraction confidence.

Extracted documentation must not be called a standards-compliant DDI merely
because it resembles one. DDI conformance requires validation against the
applicable standard and review of provenance.

## Drafting and bounded pre-approval testing

The drafting component receives only approved inputs: the data profile,
structured documentation, relevant precedents, and canonical rules. It produces
a versioned draft specification with uncertainty and evidence visible.

A draft can be syntactically executable while remaining unauthorized. This
resolves an ambiguity in older drafts: a controlled sandbox may test a draft,
but production may execute only an approved version. Sandbox iteration must be
bounded by maximum attempts, time or cost limits, permitted changes, and stop
conditions for conceptual ambiguity.

## Human review and approval

The reviewer can approve, reject, or amend each proposed decision. An amendment
creates a new draft version. Approval binds the reviewer, timestamp, comments,
schema version, and exact specification hash.

Approval is not inferred from file location, a filename, a UI state, or the
absence of objections. It is an explicit record checked by the production
orchestrator.

## Deterministic execution

The production engine verifies authorization, compatibility, and hashes before
running. It applies the approved mappings and transformations without model
inference or discretionary fallback.

Determinism depends on the full execution manifest, not the specification alone.
The same input bytes, specification, engine, dependencies, configuration, and
runtime policy must be reproducible.

## Quality assurance and failure disposition

QA compares the output with versioned structural, logical, and plausibility
rules. A failed check produces a report and blocks publication unless an
explicit, authorized exception process is later defined.

Automatic retries are permitted only when approved logic and material inputs do
not change, for example after a transient infrastructure failure. Any repair to
the specification, generated code, rule set, or transformation returns to draft
status and requires reapproval. This rule supersedes archived slides that allow
an AI agent to revise post-approval logic without human input.

## Publication and precedent admission

Publication records output hashes, lineage, QA results, approval, and release
status. Precedent admission is a separate gate. A decision becomes reusable only
if it:

- originates from an approved specification;
- is associated with a successful QA disposition;
- retains evidence, applicability context, and reviewer attribution;
- is not superseded or known to conflict with current methodology; and
- passes any additional curation criteria established by the methodology owner.

# Artifact contracts

The following contracts are implementation-neutral minimums. Their formal JSON
Schema or equivalent definitions belong with the component that implements
them, while this hub records the cross-system obligations.

| Artifact | Required minimum content |
|---|---|
| Survey source bundle | Survey ID, source URI, file hashes, format, provenance, classification, acquisition date, version |
| Data profile | Contract version, source hashes, variable metadata, approved aggregate statistics, disclosure controls, profiler version |
| Documentation record | Contract version, source references, extracted fields, confidence, language, parser version, DDI validation status |
| Harmonization specification | Contract and schema versions, survey ID, parent version, lifecycle state, source and target fields, transformation, evidence, uncertainty, validations, content hash |
| Approval record | Specification hash, reviewer identity, decision, timestamp, scope, comments, attestation method |
| Execution manifest | Run ID, input hashes, approved specification hash, engine and dependency versions, configuration, environment identity, timestamps |
| QA report | Run ID, QA policy version, checks, results, severity, evidence, overall disposition |
| Publication record | Output hashes, release status, approval and QA references, location, publication timestamp |
| Audit event | Event ID, actor, action, object and version, timestamp, outcome, correlation ID |
| Precedent record | Source decision, approval and QA lineage, context, evidence, applicability, embedding version if used, supersession status |

## Harmonization specification states

The minimum lifecycle states are:

- `draft`: editable and not authorized;
- `in_review`: frozen for a review action and not authorized;
- `approved`: immutable and authorized within its recorded scope;
- `rejected`: not authorized, with a reason;
- `superseded`: formerly approved but replaced for future runs; and
- `withdrawn`: no longer authorized because of a discovered issue.

Production authorization requires `approved` status, an exact hash match, a
valid approval record, and compatibility with the selected schema and engine.

## Mapping granularity

Archived presentation material proposes mapping the most atomic observable
concepts and deriving aggregate or categorical outputs through canonical rules.
This can improve consistency and maintainability, but it is a **Proposed**
methodological design rule until the schema owner confirms its applicability to
each module. The same applies to the archived Situation A/B/C classification of
direct, inferred, and not-mappable cases.

# Roles and decision rights

| Decision | Accountable authority | Required consultation |
|---|---|---|
| Statistical definition or derivation | GMD methodology owner | Harmonizers, schema maintainers |
| Survey-specific mapping | Designated expert reviewer | Drafting evidence and precedents |
| Specification contract | Methodology and technical owners jointly | Engine, review, QA, and audit owners |
| Production release | Authorized operational owner | Reviewer and QA owner |
| Precedent admission or withdrawal | Methodology or delegated curation owner | Reviewer, QA owner |
| Trust-boundary exception | Data owner and security authority | Methodology and technical owners |
| Infrastructure product selection | Authorized ITS and project owners | Security, operations, development team |
| Canonical architecture change | Methodology and technical owners jointly | Affected component owners |

# Proof-of-concept boundary

The archived drafts consistently propose beginning with non-welfare demographic
modules and excluding income and consumption aggregates until the approach is
evaluated. This remains **Proposed**, not an approved production scope.

A proof of concept should measure at least:

- contract validity and execution success;
- reviewer correction and rejection patterns;
- time to a reviewed decision compared with an agreed baseline;
- error detection before and after human review;
- consistency across related surveys and waves;
- retrieval relevance and citation accuracy;
- reproducibility from the execution manifest; and
- security, cost, and operational failure behavior.

Claims about annual survey volume, time savings, accuracy improvements, or
production readiness must be sourced before they appear in stakeholder material.

# Open work before implementation

1. Confirm official terminology, project sponsorship, and decision owners.
2. Complete the repository and ownership map.
3. Ratify the proof-of-concept scope and evaluation design.
4. Define formal schemas for the source bundle, profile, documentation record,
   specification, approval, execution, QA, and precedent artifacts.
5. Define field-level data classifications and permitted model payloads.
6. Define QA severity, exception, publication, and withdrawal policies.
7. Resolve the infrastructure decisions and institutional approvals recorded in
   `infrastructure-requirements.qmd`.
